Padalkar affiliations: - id: BU name: Boston University city: Boston state: MA jupyter: python3 format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../theme/advisory.scss] width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.08 center: false transition: fade auto-stretch: false footer: "AD 698 - Generation, Evaluation, and Production RAG" html-math-method: katex slide-number: c/t toc: true toc-depth: 1 self-contained-math: true fig-align: center title-slide-attributes: data-background-color: "#ffffff" data-background-image: "../theme/figures/google-deepmind-jVZ_BKzDOJg-unsplash.jpg" data-background-size: cover data-background-position: center data-background-opacity: "0.22" execute: eval: false echo: false warning: false message: false bibliography: ../references.bib csl: ../mis-quarterly.csl categories: ['RAG Evaluation', 'Reranking', 'RAGAS', 'Production RAG', 'Technical Deep Dive'] description: "Introduces Generation, Evaluation, and Production RAG through concepts, technical intuition, diagrams, and applied connections to the course analytics workflow." --- ## LangChain package setup Use Python 3.11 or 3.12 for this course. Run the `%pip` cell below in the notebook's active kernel before the examples. After installing or upgrading, restart the kernel (Colab: restart the session), then run the example cells from the top. Full embedding-model, generation, and RAGAS API examples are displayed with `eval: false`; run those in the companion notebooks. Run the companion notebooks from their setup cells: - [Baseline ingestion, chunking, retrieval, and generation](../help-code/Rag/1_rag_simpler.ipynb) - [Reranking](../help-code/Rag/2_rag_simpler.ipynb), [query decomposition](../help-code/Rag/3_rag_simpler_langsmith.ipynb), [tool-style retrieval](../help-code/Rag/4_rag_simpler_langsmith.ipynb), and [reflection](../help-code/Rag/5_rag_simpler_langsmith.ipynb) - [RAGAS evaluation](../help-code/Rag/6_ragas_evaluation.ipynb) - [Embedding comparison](../help-code/Rag/7_ragas_huggingface_model_comparison.ipynb) Helpers such as `ensure_tesla_filings` and `load_filing_documents` are defined inline in those notebooks. The comparison and serving snippets below illustrate interfaces; they require the corresponding chains and models to be initialized. --- # Building the Generator ## Context Construction Good generation depends on how context is packed: - rank and select chunks - deduplicate and compress - preserve source attribution - format prompt sections clearly --- ## Prompt Template Pattern ::: {#94d7c5c2 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate RAG_PROMPT = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template( """ You are a careful assistant. Use ONLY the context to answer. Question: {question} Context: {context} If context is insufficient, say so explicitly. """ ) ``` ::: --- ## Response Contract A production answer format typically carries: - concise claim - evidence bullets - confidence note - citations or source IDs This supports grading, auditing, and stakeholder trust. # Tesla SEC 10-K RAG Pattern ## Tesla RAG Configuration ::: {#5cd7111e .cell output-location='column' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path TESLA_RAG_CONFIG = { "ticker": "TSLA", "filing_years": list(range(2015, 2026)), "chunk_size": 1200, "chunk_overlap": 180, "embedding_model": "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", "search_type": "similarity", "search_kwargs": {"k": 6}, } PROJECT_ROOT = next( folder for folder in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents) if (folder / "_quarto.yml").is_file() ) RAG_DIR = PROJECT_ROOT / "help-code/Rag" ``` ::: The retrieval configuration fixes the chunking, embedding, and search settings so chunk IDs, retrieved years, and evaluation rows remain comparable across baseline, reranked, decomposed, reflective, and embedding-comparison variants. --- ## Ingestion and Chunking Four excerpts from Tesla's 10-K filed **January 29, 2024** (fiscal year 2023). The bundled sample preserves source metadata and normalized filing text. This is a one-filing teaching sample, not a multi-year comparison. ::: {#9768674b .cell output-location='column' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json import pandas as pd from IPython.display import display from langchain_core.documents import Document from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter sample_rows = json.loads( (RAG_DIR / "data/tesla_10k_render_sample.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8") ) docs = [Document(page_content=row["text"], metadata={ key: value for key, value in row.items() if key != "text" }) for row in sample_rows] splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=400, chunk_overlap=60) chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs) for i, doc in enumerate(chunks): doc.metadata["chunk_id"] = f"TSLA-2024-sample-{i:02d}" print(f"{len(docs)} real excerpts -> {len(chunks)} chunks") display(pd.DataFrame([{ "chunk_id": d.metadata["chunk_id"], "item": d.metadata["item"], "characters": len(d.page_content), "preview": d.page_content[:90] } for d in chunks])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4 real excerpts -> 6 chunks ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: --- ## Embeddings and Vector Store ::: {#6444c524 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings embed = HuggingFaceEmbeddings( model_name=TESLA_RAG_CONFIG["embedding_model"], encode_kwargs={"normalize_embeddings": True}, ) vs = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embed) retriever = vs.as_retriever( search_type=TESLA_RAG_CONFIG["search_type"], search_kwargs=TESLA_RAG_CONFIG["search_kwargs"], ) ``` ::: --- ## Tesla Evidence Thread Tesla's filings make RAG behavior inspectable because the same business themes appear across many years: - battery supply and cost - production ramps and factory capacity - Autopilot, AI, and regulatory risk - revenue mix across automotive, energy, services, and leasing Good answers cite both the filing year and the chunk ID, not only the generated conclusion. --- ## Small Tesla Evidence Example {.code-detail} ::: {#249cdcc6 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english") chunk_vectors = vectorizer.fit_transform([d.page_content for d in chunks]) def retrieve_sample(question, k=3): scores = cosine_similarity(vectorizer.transform([question]), chunk_vectors)[0] ranked = sorted(range(len(chunks)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i)) return [(chunks[i], float(scores[i])) for i in ranked[:k] if scores[i] > 0] question = "How could battery cell supply disruptions limit production?" ranked_hits = retrieve_sample(question) retrieved_docs = [doc for doc, score in ranked_hits] display(pd.DataFrame([{ "rank": rank, "chunk_id": d.metadata["chunk_id"], "score": round(score, 3), "text": d.page_content } for rank, (d, score) in enumerate(ranked_hits, 1)])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: This executable baseline uses TF-IDF cosine similarity (lexical overlap). Its scores are neither confidence probabilities nor dense embedding scores. The preceding FAISS example shows the full notebook alternative. --- ## LCEL RAG Chain ::: {#393c5648 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda def join_context(docs): return "\n\n".join( f"[{d.metadata['chunk_id']} | Item {d.metadata['item']}] {d.page_content}" for d in docs ) sample_prompt_chain = RunnableLambda(lambda x: { "question": x["question"], "context": join_context([d for d, _ in retrieve_sample(x["question"])]) }) | RAG_PROMPT formatted_prompt = sample_prompt_chain.invoke({"question": question}) print(formatted_prompt.to_string()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Human: You are a careful assistant. Use ONLY the context to answer. Question: How could battery cell supply disruptions limit production? Context: [TSLA-2024-sample-01 | Item 1A] to date fully qualified only a very limited number of such suppliers and have limited flexibility in changing suppliers. Any disruption in the supply of battery cells from our suppliers could limit production of our vehicles and energy storage products. [TSLA-2024-sample-00 | Item 1A] We are dependent on the continued supply of lithium-ion battery cells for our vehicles and energy storage products, and we will require substantially more cells to grow our business according to our plans. Currently, we rely on suppliers such as Panasonic and Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) for these cells. We have to date fully qualified only a very limited number of such [TSLA-2024-sample-02 | Item 1A] We have previously experienced and may in the future experience launch and production ramp delays for new products and features. For example, we encountered unanticipated supplier issues that led to delays during the initial ramp of our first Model X and experienced challenges with a supplier and with ramping full automation for certain of our initial Model 3 manufacturing processes. In addition, If context is insufficient, say so explicitly. ``` ::: ::: --- ## A Cited Extractive Answer This output selects an exact sentence from the retrieved evidence. It is an extractive answer, not an LLM-generated synthesis. ::: {#96905846 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import re def extract_sample_answer(question): hits = retrieve_sample(question) if not hits: return "The sample contains insufficient evidence." candidates = [(sentence, doc.metadata["chunk_id"]) for doc, _ in hits for sentence in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", doc.page_content) if sentence.endswith((".", "!", "?"))] if not candidates: return "The sample contains insufficient evidence." scores = cosine_similarity( vectorizer.transform([question]), vectorizer.transform([sentence for sentence, _ in candidates]) )[0] best = int(scores.argmax()) sentence, citation = candidates[best] return f"{sentence} [{citation}]" sample_answer = extract_sample_answer(question) print(sample_answer) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Any disruption in the supply of battery cells from our suppliers could limit production of our vehicles and energy storage products. [TSLA-2024-sample-01] ``` ::: ::: --- ## Evaluate the Sample Retrieval For each question, mark one excerpt relevant by hand. Precision@3 measures relevant chunks among the three returned; recall@3 measures coverage of that excerpt's chunks. These are **sample retrieval metrics**, not RAGAS or semantic faithfulness scores. ::: {#65655ad8 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} sample_questions = [ ("How could battery cell supply disruptions limit production?", "battery-supply"), ("What launch and production ramp delays were experienced?", "production-ramp"), ("How does Tesla sell directly and support customers?", "customer-network"), ] evaluation_rows = [] for query, relevant_sample in sample_questions: relevant_ids = {d.metadata["chunk_id"] for d in chunks if d.metadata["sample_id"] == relevant_sample} found_ids = {d.metadata["chunk_id"] for d, _ in retrieve_sample(query, k=3)} hits = len(found_ids & relevant_ids) evaluation_rows.append({ "target_excerpt": relevant_sample, "precision@3": round(hits / 3, 2), "recall@3": round(hits / len(relevant_ids), 2), "retrieved_ids": ", ".join(sorted(found_ids)), }) display(pd.DataFrame(evaluation_rows)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
target_excerpt precision@3 recall@3 retrieved_ids
0 battery-supply 0.67 1.0 TSLA-2024-sample-00, TSLA-2024-sample-01, TSLA...
1 production-ramp 0.33 0.5 TSLA-2024-sample-01, TSLA-2024-sample-02
2 customer-network 0.33 1.0 TSLA-2024-sample-04
``` ::: ::: Try changing `chunk_size`, `chunk_overlap`, or the question wording and inspect which evidence moves into or out of the top three. --- ## RAG Is Not Magic RAG improves the odds of grounded answers, but it adds new system risks. | Benefit | New responsibility | |---|---| | fresher evidence | keep the index current | | citations | preserve metadata and source IDs | | better factuality | evaluate retrieval and generation separately | | domain control | monitor corpus quality and access rules | The practical question is not "Did we add RAG?" It is "Did retrieval improve the answer enough to justify complexity, latency, and maintenance?" # Evaluation and Diagnostics ## A Practical Evaluation Matrix Track both quality and operations: - answer relevance - groundedness / faithfulness - citation quality - latency - cost per query - retrieval hit quality --- ## Baseline vs RAG Evaluation For each SEC question, compare: 1. prompt-only answer 2. RAG answer 3. retrieved evidence table Diagnostic questions: - Did RAG cite better evidence? - Did it reduce unsupported claims? - Did it introduce irrelevant or stale context? - Did the extra latency and complexity produce business value? --- # From Classification Evaluation to RAG Evaluation ## How We Usually Evaluate Classifiers For a classifier, evaluation starts with a confusion matrix: | | predicted positive | predicted negative | |---|---:|---:| | actual positive | TP | FN | | actual negative | FP | TN | Common metrics: $$ \begin{align} \text{Accuracy}&=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN},\\ \text{Precision}&=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\\ \text{Recall}&=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\\ F_1&=\frac{2PR}{P+R} \end{align} $$ --- ## Where Classification Metrics Fail for RAG :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Classification assumes: - fixed label set - one prediction per record - ground truth labels available - correctness can be reduced to match / mismatch ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} RAG violates those assumptions: - answers are open-ended text - the same answer can be partially correct - unsupported true claims are still risky - retrieval can fail even when generation looks fluent - generation can fail even when retrieval found good evidence ::: :::: For SEC analysis, "sounds right" is not enough. The claim must be traceable. --- ## RAG Needs Multi-Axis Evaluation Evaluate the pipeline, not only the final paragraph. | Layer | Question | Typical failure | |---|---|---| | Retrieval | Did we fetch useful evidence? | wrong item, wrong year, noisy chunk | | Grounding | Is the answer supported? | hallucinated or uncited claim | | Relevance | Did it answer the question? | fluent but off-target answer | | Operations | Can we run it reliably? | high latency, high cost, brittle index | RAGAS formalizes the first three quality dimensions for automated review. --- ## Why Text Overlap Is Not Enough Traditional NLP metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and semantic similarity can be useful for summaries or translations, but they miss two questions that matter in RAG: - did the system retrieve the evidence needed to answer? - is every answer claim supported by that evidence? A response can share many words with a reference and still cite the wrong filing section. A response can also be semantically similar to a reference while adding an unsupported financial claim. This is why modern RAG evaluation treats the response as a set of claims and the retriever as a ranked evidence system. --- # RAGAS Evaluation ## RAGAS Paper: Core Idea RAGAS [@RAGAS2023] began as a reference-free framework for evaluating RAG systems, then evolved into a broader evaluation toolkit for retrieval, generation, agents, and workflows. Given: - question: $q$ - retrieved context: $c(q)$ - generated answer: $a_s(q)$ The original RAGAS paper focuses on three core ideas: 1. **faithfulness**: is the answer grounded in context? 2. **answer relevance**: does the answer address the question? 3. **context relevance**: is the retrieved context focused? --- ## RAGAS Data Model The current Ragas examples organize each evaluation row around four practical fields: | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `user_input` | the original user question | | `response` | the generated answer | | `retrieved_contexts` | ranked chunks used by the RAG system | | `reference` | optional ground-truth answer or instructor-approved evidence summary | That schema is useful even without the library. It forces every row to preserve both the final answer and the evidence path. --- ## Metric Map | Metric | Evaluates | Needs | Reference-free? | |---|---|---|---| | faithfulness | answer support | user input, response, contexts | yes | | answer relevancy | answer-to-question fit | user input, response | yes | | context utilization | useful retrieved context | user input, response, contexts | yes | | context precision | ranked evidence quality | user input, contexts, reference | usually no | | context recall | evidence coverage | user input, contexts, reference | no | | answer correctness | answer vs reference | user input, response, reference | no | | noise sensitivity | effect of irrelevant context | user input, response, contexts, reference | no | Generation metrics and retrieval metrics belong together. High answer quality with poor retrieval may be luck. Good retrieval with poor answer quality is a synthesis problem. --- ## Faithfulness: Math Break the generated answer into claims: $$ S(a_s(q))=\{s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n\} $$ Let $V$ be the subset of claims that can be inferred from retrieved context $c(q)$. $$ \text{Faithfulness}=\frac{|V|}{|S(a_s(q))|} $$ Example: - Claim 1: "Tesla discusses battery supply as important to production scale." supported - Claim 2: "Tesla says battery costs doubled in 2024." not supported $$ \text{Faithfulness}=\frac{1}{2}=0.50 $$ --- ## Faithfulness: Minimal Judge Pattern ::: {#2f45da1e .cell output-location='column' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} faithfulness_prompt = """ Extract factual claims from the answer. For each claim, decide if it is supported by the context. Return JSON with claim, supported, and reason. Question: {question} Context: {context} Answer: {answer} """ ``` ::: Interpretation: - high score: most claims can be traced to retrieved evidence - low score: answer may be hallucinated, overgeneralized, or missing citations --- ## Answer Relevancy: Math RAGAS estimates whether the answer fits the original question. Process: 1. Generate synthetic questions from the answer. 2. Embed each synthetic question and the original question. 3. Average cosine similarity. $$ \text{AnswerRelevance} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \cos(E_{g_i}, E_q) $$ where $g_i$ is a generated question implied by the answer. The answer can be faithful but still irrelevant if it cites true context that does not answer the user. --- ## Context Recall Context recall asks whether retrieved context covers the reference answer. Break ground truth into claims: $$ G=\{g_1,g_2,\ldots,g_m\} $$ Let $A$ be the subset of ground-truth claims attributable to retrieved context. $$ \text{ContextRecall}=\frac{|A|}{|G|} $$ Example: - ground truth claim 1: Tesla discusses production ramp risk supported - ground truth claim 2: Tesla connects that risk to specific factory capacity changes not retrieved $$ \text{ContextRecall}=\frac{1}{2}=0.50 $$ --- ## Context Precision Context precision asks whether useful chunks appear early in the ranked retrieval list. For retrieved chunks ranked $1 \ldots K$: $$ P@k=\frac{\text{relevant chunks in top }k}{k} $$ Average precision over relevant chunks: $$ \text{ContextPrecision@K} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{k=1}^{K} P@k \cdot rel_k $$ where $rel_k=1$ if chunk $k$ is relevant. This catches the "right evidence buried under noise" problem. --- ## Answer Correctness Answer correctness compares the generated response with a reference answer. Ragas combines two ideas: - **factual similarity**: claim overlap between response and reference - **semantic similarity**: embedding similarity between response and reference For factual overlap: $$ \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \quad \text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} $$ $$ F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R} $$ In a finance workflow, this becomes useful when a gold evidence summary exists, such as an analyst-approved answer or a curated evaluation set. --- ## Noise Sensitivity Noise sensitivity asks whether the system is distracted by retrieved content that is related but not actually useful. $$ \text{NoiseSensitivity} = \frac{\text{incorrect claims in response}}{\text{total claims in response}} $$ Lower is better. Example: - context includes a correct Autopilot regulatory-risk passage and an unrelated energy-storage paragraph - answer incorrectly says Autopilot regulation caused energy-storage revenue growth - the error is not simply low relevance; it is sensitivity to distracting context This metric is valuable when comparing baseline RAG with reranking, query decomposition, and reflection. --- ## Sample RAGAS Dataset RAGAS expects one row per question. ::: {#fbd78bd6 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from ragas import EvaluationDataset eval_rows = [{ "user_input": "How did Tesla describe battery technology, battery costs, or battery supply across the filings?", "response": rag_answer, "retrieved_contexts": [doc.page_content for doc in retrieved_docs], "reference": ( "A strong answer compares multiple years and cites evidence about " "battery technology, battery cost, supply constraints, production " "scale, and energy storage or vehicle battery strategy." ), }] eval_dataset = EvaluationDataset.from_list(eval_rows) ``` ::: Without `reference`, start with faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context utilization. --- ## Running RAGAS Metrics {.code-detail} ::: {#47dd87a3 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} from ragas import evaluate from ragas.metrics import ( Faithfulness, ResponseRelevancy, LLMContextPrecisionWithReference, LLMContextRecall, FactualCorrectness, NoiseSensitivity, ) ``` ::: ## Evaluating with RAGAS {.code-detail} ::: {#7ffef583 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} scores = evaluate( dataset=eval_dataset, metrics=[ Faithfulness(), ResponseRelevancy(), LLMContextPrecisionWithReference(), LLMContextRecall(), FactualCorrectness(), NoiseSensitivity(), ], llm=evaluator_llm, embeddings=evaluator_embeddings, ) scores.to_pandas() ``` ::: --- ## Comparing RAG Variants RAG systems improve by changing one design choice at a time, then measuring the effect on evidence quality, answer quality, and latency. | Variant | System change | Expected effect | |---|---|---| | Baseline RAG | retrieve top chunks, then answer | clear evidence path and a simple quality floor | | Reranked RAG | reorder candidate chunks before generation | stronger context precision when similarity search returns noisy passages | | Query decomposition | split a complex question into focused subqueries | better coverage for multi-year or multi-part questions | | Tool-style RAG | route retrieval through explicit search tools | clearer control over all-year, single-year, early-year, and recent-year evidence | | Reflective RAG | review and revise the first answer | fewer unsupported claims, with added latency | | Embedding comparison | hold the corpus fixed and change embeddings | different tradeoffs among coverage, ranking quality, and speed | The best design depends on the failure mode: missed evidence, noisy ranking, unsupported synthesis, or excessive latency. --- ## Experiment Harness for Model Variants {.code-detail} ::: {#42040c74 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} TESLA_EVAL_QUESTIONS = [ { "qid": "q1_battery_technology", "user_input": "How did Tesla describe battery technology, battery costs, or battery supply across the filings?", "reference": ( "A strong answer compares multiple years and cites evidence about " "battery technology, battery cost, supply constraints, production " "scale, and energy storage or vehicle battery strategy." ), "reference_keywords": ["battery", "cost", "supply", "technology", "production"], }, { "qid": "q2_manufacturing_capacity", "user_input": "How did Tesla's manufacturing capacity and production ramp risks evolve from 2015 through 2025?", "reference": ( "A strong answer discusses production ramp, manufacturing capacity, " "factories, scaling risk, delivery volume, and operational execution." ), "reference_keywords": ["manufacturing", "production", "capacity", "factory", "ramp"], }, ] ``` ::: ## Configuring Model Variants {.code-detail} ::: {#2093e53e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} rag_variants = { "baseline": baseline_rag, "reranker": reranker_rag, "query_decomp": query_decomposer_rag, "react": react_rag, "reflection": reflection_rag, } ``` ::: ## Collecting Variant Results {.code-detail} ::: {#21a5e083 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} rows = [] for name, chain in rag_variants.items(): for item in TESLA_EVAL_QUESTIONS: result = chain.invoke({"input": item["user_input"]}) rows.append({ "variant": name, "qid": item["qid"], "user_input": item["user_input"], "response": result["answer"], "retrieved_contexts": [d.page_content for d in result["context"]], "retrieved_chunk_ids": [d.metadata["chunk_id"] for d in result["context"]], "retrieved_years": [d.metadata["filing_year"] for d in result["context"]], "reference": item["reference"], "latency_ms": result.get("latency_ms"), }) variant_eval_df = pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: The evaluation table preserves the answer, retrieved evidence, source years, references, and latency for each variant. --- ## Hugging Face Embedding Comparison {.code-detail} The embedding comparison keeps the Tesla corpus, questions, generator, and metrics fixed while changing only the embedding model. ::: {#19512c7a .cell output-location='column' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} HF_EMBEDDING_OPTIONS = { "minilm_l6": "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", "mpnet_base": "sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2", "bge_small": "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5", "bge_base": "BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5", } ``` ::: ## Comparing Embedding Retrieval {.code-detail} ::: {#a3220c58 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} comparison_rows = [] for option_name, model_name in HF_EMBEDDING_OPTIONS.items(): vector_store = build_vector_store(model_name) retriever = vector_store.as_retriever( search_type="mmr", search_kwargs={"k": 8, "fetch_k": 32}, ) for item in TESLA_EVAL_QUESTIONS: docs_for_q = retriever.invoke(item["user_input"]) comparison_rows.append({ "option": option_name, "qid": item["qid"], "retrieved_chunk_ids": [d.metadata["chunk_id"] for d in docs_for_q], "retrieved_years": [d.metadata["filing_year"] for d in docs_for_q], "retrieved_contexts": [d.page_content for d in docs_for_q], "reference": item["reference"], }) comparison_df = pd.DataFrame(comparison_rows) ``` ::: `retrieved_chunk_ids` and `retrieved_years` make retrieval differences visible before the generated answers are scored. --- ## Interpreting the Evaluation Table | Pattern | Likely diagnosis | Fix | |---|---|---| | low context recall | missing evidence | increase $k$, improve chunking, rewrite query | | low context precision | noisy ranking | add reranker or metadata filters | | low faithfulness | unsupported generation | stricter prompt, citations, lower temperature | | low answer relevance | off-target synthesis | rewrite prompt or decompose query | | low answer correctness | mismatches reference | improve retrieval coverage or final synthesis | | high noise sensitivity | distracted by nearby context | rerank, filter, reduce $k$, compress context | | high quality, high latency | costly pipeline | cache, reduce context, simplify chain | RAGAS-style scores are triage signals. They identify rows that need closer inspection, especially when the answer makes financial claims. --- ## Evaluation Loop A production RAG workflow improves through repeated measurement: 1. build a small, representative question set 2. run each RAG variant against the same questions 3. store responses, retrieved contexts, references, latency, and cost 4. score retrieval and generation separately 5. inspect the worst rows before changing the system Across RAG evaluation implementations, the durable artifact is the evaluation table itself: each row preserves the question, generated response, retrieved evidence, optional reference answer, metric scores, latency, and cost. --- ## LLM-as-a-Judge Loop ::: {#17753b04 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} judge_prompt = """ Rate the answer from 1-5 for groundedness and relevance. Question: {q} Answer: {a} Reference: {ref} Return JSON. """ ``` ::: Sampled human checks calibrate the judge and help detect drift. --- ## Error Taxonomy - retrieval miss: right info absent - retrieval noise: irrelevant chunk dominates - synthesis failure: answer conflicts with evidence - abstention failure: answer needed an "insufficient context" response Each error type implies a different fix path. # Productionization ## Serving with LangServe + FastAPI ::: {#dd249f87 .cell output-location='column' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} from fastapi import FastAPI from langserve import add_routes app = FastAPI(title="AD698-RAG") add_routes(app, chain, path="/rag") ``` ::: The same chain can be exposed behind an endpoint while preserving the retrieval trace and response contract. --- ## Observability Checklist - log query, retrieved chunk IDs, and latency - store prompt and response traces - monitor bad-case cohorts - keep versioned index snapshots - maintain rollback strategy --- ## Security and Governance - content filtering on user input/output - source allowlist and document sanitation - secret management for model keys - PII-safe logging and retention policy # Wrap-Up ## Key Takeaways - Retrieval quality gates generation quality - Evaluation must cover quality and operations - Production RAG requires traceability, not just fluency - RAGAS-style metrics separate evidence retrieval from answer generation ---
